pos: n. (the former Augustinian friary church in London, granted to the Dutch congregation in 1550)
etymology: Austin, the English contraction of Augustine; friar from Latin frater, a brother, through Old French frere.
biblical_def: Austin Friars was the London house of the Augustinian friars, dissolved with the rest in 1538, and on 24 July 1550 Edward VI granted its nave by letters patent to the Protestant strangers in London — the Dutch, German and Walloon refugees — to be their temple, with John a Lasco as superintendent and liberty to use their own rites and discipline. The charter is a remarkable document: a Reformed king gave foreigners a church building, their own confession, their own consistory, and exemption from the English ordinary, which is to say he recognised them as churches rather than tolerating them as guests. The French-speaking congregation soon took separate premises in Threadneedle Street; the Dutch kept Austin Friars, and keep it still, the oldest Dutch-language church in the world, rebuilt after the German bombing of 1940. For four centuries it has been the point to which persecuted Netherlanders came. “for mine house shall be called an house of prayer for all people” (Isa 56:7).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a friary as a monastery or convent of friars, and letters patent as a writing conferring a right or privilege.
webster_full: FRI'ARY, n. A monastery or convent of friars; a brotherhood.
LET'TERS PATENT, A writing executed and sealed, by which power and authority are conferred.
TEM'PLE, n. A public edifice erected to the worship of God; a church.

corruption_summary: A dissolved friary given to refugees, and still their church after four centuries.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The live misuse is the reading of the 1550 charter as an early act of religious toleration in the modern sense, a state making room for diversity. Edward's council did nothing so vague. It recognised specific Reformed congregations holding a Reformed confession and exercising a Reformed discipline, and withheld the same liberty from others.

The principle to recover is that the house of God is for the nations by promise and not by concession: “for mine house shall be called an house of prayer for all people” (Isa 56:7). Solomon's dedication prayer had already made express provision for the foreigner who came for the name's sake — “Moreover concerning a stranger, that is not of thy people Israel, but cometh out of a far country for thy name's sake” (1Ki 8:41) — which is exactly what the refugees at Austin Friars were.

pos: n. (the Dutch stranger congregation at Austin Friars, founded 1550)
etymology: Dutch, from Middle Dutch duutsch, of the people; the congregation's own name was the Nederduytsche gemeynte.
biblical_def: The Dutch Church of London was the largest and most important of the stranger congregations, and the one that mattered most to the history of Reformed church order. Gathered at Austin Friars in 1550 under John a Lasco as superintendent, with Martin Micron and Jan Utenhove among its officers, it was the first congregation anywhere to operate a complete Reformed polity in a country that had not adopted one: a confession of its own, a consistory of ministers and elders with real disciplinary power, deacons for the poor, catechising, and the fencing of the table. A Lasco wrote the order down in his Forma ac ratio, which was printed abroad and became a working pattern for the Dutch churches at home when they could at last be organised, and which influenced the English Puritans who could see it functioning three streets from St Paul's. Mary's accession in 1553 dispersed the congregation across the North Sea; it re-formed under Elizabeth and has never since been dissolved. “And when they had ordained them elders in every church, and had prayed with fasting, they commended them to the Lord” (Act 14:23).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a consistory as an assembly of ecclesiastical persons for regulating affairs, and polity as the form of civil or ecclesiastical government.
webster_full: CON'SISTORY, n. A place of justice in the spiritual court; an assembly of ecclesiastical persons.
POL'ITY, n. The form or constitution of civil government; the constitution of a church.
DEA'CON, n. A person in the lowest degree of holy orders; an officer for the care of the poor.
DIS'CIPLINE, n. The exercise of government and correction over the members of a church.

corruption_summary: The first complete Reformed polity in a country that had not adopted one.
corruption_paragraphs: The modern account treats the stranger churches as a curiosity of Tudor administration, an immigrant chaplaincy. They were nothing of the kind, and the English bishops who first welcomed them understood it better than later historians: here was a church ordering itself by elders and discipline rather than by ordinary and canon law, within a mile of Lambeth, and doing it visibly. That is why Grindal supervised them carefully and why the Puritans cited them.

The principle to recover is that church discipline is an ordinance of Christ exercised over those within and not over the world: “For what have I to do to judge them also that are without? do not ye judge them that are within?” (1Co 5:12). The Lord's own procedure ends in the congregation and not in a magistrate's court: “And if he shall neglect to hear them, tell it unto the church” (Mat 18:17).

pos: n. (the French and Walloon stranger congregation in London, founded 1550)
etymology: French, of France, from Germanic Frank; the congregation's long home was in Threadneedle Street.
biblical_def: The French Church of London was chartered with the Dutch in Edward VI's grant of 1550 and soon took separate premises, settling at last in Threadneedle Street, where it remained for three centuries. Its first ministers were François Perussel and Richard Vauville; Valerand Poullain served it; Nicolas des Gallars was sent from Geneva to it in 1560 at Bishop Grindal's own request and drew up its revised discipline with Calvin's advice. Dispersed under Mary and re-gathered under Elizabeth, it received wave upon wave: Walloons fleeing Alva in the 1560s, Huguenots after the massacre of 1572, and the great flood after the Revocation of the Edict of Nantes in 1685, when it and its daughter congregations absorbed tens of thousands into Spitalfields and Soho. It is the longest continuous French Protestant congregation outside France and the institutional heart of the Huguenot refuge in England. “behold, I have set before thee an open door, and no man can shut it” (Rev 3:8).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a refugee as one who flies to a shelter or place of safety, and a Walloon as one of the people of the southern Netherlands.
webster_full: REFUGEE', n. One who flies to a shelter or place of safety; one who in times of persecution flees to a foreign country.
WALLOON', n. One of a people inhabiting the southern provinces of the Netherlands; their dialect of French.
CON'GREGATION, n. An assembly of persons met for the worship of God.
DOOR, n. An opening or passage; access; means of approach or entrance.

corruption_summary: Threadneedle Street, the institutional heart of the Huguenot refuge.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The live misuse is the modern framing of the Huguenot refuge as an immigration story told in economic terms: skilled weavers and silversmiths enriching the English trades. They did; and they came because men with knives were hunting them, and the first thing they asked for on arrival was a church where the word was preached in their own tongue.

The principle to recover is that the scattering of the church has always been one of God's means of planting it: “Now they which were scattered abroad upon the persecution that arose about Stephen travelled as far as Phenice, and Cyprus, and Antioch, preaching the word” (Act 11:19). Luke records the result without comment on the method: “And the hand of the Lord was with them: and a great number believed, and turned unto the Lord” (Act 11:21).

pos: n. (Martin Micron, c. 1523–1559, physician and minister of the Dutch Church of London, chronicler of the exiles' voyage)
etymology: Latin Martinus, of Mars, warlike; Micron, a grecised form of his family name de Cleyne, the little.
biblical_def: Martin Micron was a Ghent man who studied medicine at Basel, came to London as a physician, and was made one of the ministers of the Dutch congregation at Austin Friars under John a Lasco. He wrote De christelicke ordinancien, a plain Dutch description of that congregation's order of worship and discipline, which carried the London pattern to the Netherlands. When Mary came to the throne in 1553 he was one of the leaders of the company of about a hundred and seventy-five exiles who took ship for Denmark; the Danish Lutheran authorities refused them a landing unless they would subscribe the Lutheran doctrine of the Supper, and they would not. They were turned away from Copenhagen, then from Rostock, Wismar and Lübeck in the winter, and were finally received at Emden. Micron served there and died at Norden in 1559. The dictionary records the Danish refusal plainly: Protestants shut Protestants out into a Baltic winter over the Supper. “they wandered in deserts, and in mountains, and in dens and caves of the earth” (Heb 11:38).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines to sojourn as to dwell for a time, and to receive as to take, admit, or welcome.
webster_full: SO'JOURN, v. To dwell for a time; to live in a place as a temporary resident.
RECEIVE', v. To take, as a thing offered; to admit; to welcome; to entertain.
OR'DINANCE, n. An established rite or ceremony; a rule established by authority.
PHYSI'CIAN, n. A person skilled in the art of healing.

corruption_summary: The minister turned away from four Lutheran ports in the winter of 1553.
corruption_paragraphs: It is often argued that the sacramental controversies of the sixteenth century were an academic dispute that touched no one outside the universities. The voyage of 1553 is the answer. A hundred and seventy-five people, including women and children, were refused harbour in one Protestant port after another in a Baltic winter because their ministers would not subscribe a Lutheran formula on the Lord's Supper. Doctrine had consequences in the flesh, and the party that made it cost blood was not the party that refused to sign.

The principle to recover is the plain apostolic command that governs the treatment of brethren who differ within the faith, and that Copenhagen and Lübeck broke: “Wherefore receive ye one another, as Christ also received us to the glory of God” (Rom 15:7). The measure of the hospitality owed is the reception Christ gave, and nothing less was asked of those ports.

pos: n. (Jan Utenhove, c. 1516–1566, Flemish nobleman, elder of the Dutch Church of London, translator of the Dutch New Testament and Psalms)
etymology: Dutch Jan, from Hebrew Yochanan, the LORD is gracious; Utenhove, from the court, of a patrician house of Ghent.
biblical_def: Jan Utenhove was a patrician of Ghent who left the Netherlands in 1544 for the faith and spent the rest of his life among the exiles, in Strasbourg, London, Emden and Poland. He was never ordained; he served the Dutch Church of London as an elder, and his work was the people's singing and the people's Bible. He put the Psalms into Dutch metre, published in instalments from 1551, which gave the Dutch Reformed their first metrical psalter and were sung in the churches of the Netherlands for a generation; and he translated the whole New Testament into Dutch from the Greek, printed at Emden in 1556, the first Dutch New Testament made from the original. He also wrote the history of the 1553 voyage of the exiles, the fullest account of it. He died in London in 1566, an elder to the last. The two things he gave his people were a Testament they could read and psalms they could sing. “Speaking to yourselves in psalms and hymns and spiritual songs, singing and making melody in your heart to the Lord” (Eph 5:19).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a psalter as the book of Psalms, and metre as the measured arrangement of syllables in verse.
webster_full: PSAL'TER, n. The book of Psalms; often applied to a psalm-book for singing.
ME'TRE, n. The arrangement of a certain number of syllables in a certain order; measure; verse.
EL'DER, n. In the primitive church, one who had the oversight and care of a church.
MEL'ODY, n. An agreeable succession of sounds; a tune.

corruption_summary: The elder who gave the Dutch their first metrical psalter and their first Greek-based Testament.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The live misuse is a modern condescension toward metrical psalmody as a crude expedient of an age without hymns. Utenhove's psalters were not a makeshift. They were an attempt to put the inspired songbook of the church into the mouths of farmers and weavers in their own measure, and the congregations that learned them sang their way through Alva's terror.

The principle to recover is that congregational singing is commanded and that its matter is given: “Speaking to yourselves in psalms and hymns and spiritual songs” (Eph 5:19). James makes it the ordinary outlet of a settled heart as prayer is of an afflicted one — “Is any merry? let him sing psalms” (Jam 5:13) — and the psalmist sets the term of the obligation: “I will sing unto the LORD as long as I live” (Psa 104:33).

pos: n. (Valerand Poullain, c. 1520–1557, Walloon minister in London and Glastonbury, author of the Liturgia Sacra)
etymology: French Valerand, from Latin Valerandus, to be strong; Poullain, a colt, from Old French poulain.
biblical_def: Valerand Poullain was a Walloon of Lille, a man of some birth who was ordained in the Roman church and came over to the Reformation; he served the French congregation at Strasbourg after Calvin left it, quarrelled with Calvin over a disputed marriage and was reconciled, and came to England in 1548. He ministered to the French-speaking strangers in London and then, in 1551, led a colony of Walloon weavers to Glastonbury under the Duke of Somerset's successor as superintendent of their church. His chief work is the Liturgia Sacra, published at London in 1551 and again at Frankfurt: a complete Reformed order of worship in Latin and French, drawn from Strasbourg and Geneva, which was the fullest statement of Reformed liturgical practice then available in England and which left marks on the thinking of the English Puritans about the shape of a service. He died at Frankfurt in 1557. “Let all things be done decently and in order” (1Co 14:40).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a liturgy as a form of prayers and ceremonies used in public worship, and order as regular disposition, settled mode of proceeding.
webster_full: LIT'URGY, n. A form of prayers and ceremonial observances used in the public worship of God.
OR'DER, n. Regular disposition; methodical arrangement; established mode of proceeding.
DE'CENTLY, adv. In a decent or becoming manner; with propriety of behaviour.
EDIFICA'TION, n. The act of building up, in a moral sense; instruction; improvement of the mind.
scriptures: Let all things be done decently and in order.
How is it then, brethren? when ye come together, every one of you hath a psalm, hath a doctrine, hath a tongue, hath a revelation, hath an interpretation. Let all things be done unto edifying.

corruption_summary: The Walloon who wrote a Reformed service book and led weavers to Glastonbury.
corruption_paragraphs: Poullain's book bears on a dispute that is still live: whether a Reformed church may have a set liturgy at all, or whether the regulative principle requires that every part of worship be free. The dictionary's position follows the Liturgia Sacra itself. Scripture prescribes the elements of worship and leaves the order to be arranged for edification, so that a form which contains nothing but commanded elements, arranged decently, is not an imposition but an aid, and a congregation left wholly to a minister's improvisation is not thereby freer.

The principle to recover is Paul's own, given at the end of the longest passage in Scripture on the conduct of a service, and given as a command: “Let all things be done decently and in order” (1Co 14:40). The purpose that governs the arrangement is named a few verses earlier: “Let all things be done unto edifying” (1Co 14:26).

pos: n. pl. (the Walloon weaving colony and congregation planted at Glastonbury in 1551)
etymology: Glastonbury, the stronghold of the Glastings, in Somerset; weaver, one who weaves, from Old English wefan.
biblical_def: The Glastonbury weavers were a colony of Walloon Protestant cloth-workers settled on the lands of the dissolved abbey of Glastonbury in 1551, with Valerand Poullain as the superintendent of their church. The scheme was a double one, and both halves were deliberate: England wanted the Walloons' skill in the fine broadcloth it was then importing, and the Protector's government wanted to shelter persecuted Reformed artisans. Some forty households came, with looms, a minister, elders and deacons, and a congregation worshipping by Poullain's own order. The whole thing lasted two years. Mary's accession in 1553 ended it; the colony was broken up, the weavers scattered to Frankfurt and the Rhine, and Poullain went with them. It is the first planned Protestant refugee settlement in English history and the ancestor of every later one, down to Spitalfields and Canterbury and Norwich. “Build ye houses, and dwell in them; and plant gardens, and eat the fruit of them” (Jer 29:5).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a colony as a company of people transplanted from their mother country, and a loom as a frame or machine for weaving cloth.
webster_full: COL'ONY, n. A company or body of people transplanted from their mother country to a remote province.

BROAD'CLOTH, n. A species of woollen cloth of a fine texture and a broad width.
SO'JOURNER, n. A temporary resident; a stranger or traveller who dwells in a place for a time.

corruption_summary: Forty Walloon households, their looms and their minister, planted and scattered in two years.
corruption_paragraphs: The Glastonbury scheme is cited in modern writing as an early instance of economic migration policy, which is true and insufficient. The government wanted broadcloth; it is also the case that the people it brought over were being hunted in the Low Countries, that it gave them a church with its own discipline and a minister of their own choosing, and that it did so because the men then governing England were Reformed and thought such people had a claim on them.

The principle to recover is the law of Israel toward the stranger, which is not a sentiment but a statute with a reason attached: “But the stranger that dwelleth with you shall be unto you as one born among you, and thou shalt love him as thyself; for ye were strangers in the land of Egypt” (Lev 19:34). Jeremiah's word to exiles tells them to put down roots rather than wait: “Build ye houses, and dwell in them” (Jer 29:5). The Glastonbury weavers obeyed it and had two years.

pos: n. (Adrian van Haemstede, c. 1525–1562, minister of the Dutch Church of London, author of the first Dutch martyrology)
etymology: Latin Hadrianus, of Hadria; van Haemstede, of Haamstede in Zeeland.
biblical_def: Adrian van Haemstede was a Zeelander who preached to the hidden congregations of Antwerp at the height of the persecution and then came to London as a minister of the Dutch Church at Austin Friars. In 1559 he published at Emden De Geschiedenisse ende den doodt der vromer Martelaren, the first Dutch martyrology, drawn partly from his own knowledge of the Antwerp deaths; it went through many editions and did for the Netherlands what Foxe did for England. The next year he quarrelled with his own consistory and with Bishop Grindal. He had received some Antwerp Anabaptists into fellowship, pleading that they erred on the person of Christ out of ignorance and should be borne with as weak brethren; the consistory held that a denial of Christ's true humanity is not a weakness but a heresy, and when he would not retract he was excommunicated and banished, and died at Emden in 1562. The dictionary honours the martyrologist and sides with the consistory. “Him that is weak in the faith receive ye, but not to doubtful disputations” (Rom 14:1).

WEAK, a. Feeble in mind or intellect; not well supported by argument or evidence.
ADMONI'TION, n. Gentle reproof; counselling against fault or error; warning.

A man that is an heretick after the first and second admonition reject;
Now I beseech you, brethren, mark them which cause divisions and offences contrary to the doctrine which ye have learned; and avoid them.
And if any man obey not our word by this epistle, note that man, and have no company with him, that he may be ashamed.
corruption_summary: The martyrologist excommunicated for calling an error about Christ a weakness.
corruption_paragraphs: The Haemstede case is a favourite of modern writing on toleration, in which he is the generous man and the consistory a company of inquisitors who had learned nothing from the martyrs they had just buried. The framing will not survive the detail. What was at issue was not baptism or the magistracy but whether Christ took true flesh of the Virgin, and the Antwerp men in question denied it. A congregation of refugees from the Inquisition still had to say what it believed about the incarnation.

The principle to recover is that Scripture distinguishes the weak brother from the heretic and prescribes different treatment for each. The weak are to be received: “Him that is weak in the faith receive ye, but not to doubtful disputations” (Rom 14:1). The man who holds and spreads a fundamental error is to be dealt with otherwise, and patiently, but finally: “A man that is an heretick after the first and second admonition reject” (Tit 3:10). Charity is not the collapse of the distinction.

pos: n. (Nicolas des Gallars, c. 1520–1581, Calvin's colleague, minister of the French Church of London)
etymology: French Nicolas, from Greek Nikolaos, victory of the people; des Gallars, a seigneurial name, latinised Gallasius.
biblical_def: Nicolas des Gallars was one of the ministers of Geneva and among Calvin's closest helpers: he edited Calvin's works, translated several into French and Latin, and acted as his secretary and representative. In 1557 he was sent to Paris to strengthen the congregation there after the raid in the rue Saint-Jacques; in 1560 Geneva lent him to London at the request of Edmund Grindal, Bishop of London, to take charge of the French stranger congregation, which had fallen into disorder. He stayed about three years, settled the quarrels, and drew up with Grindal's concurrence a revised discipline, the Forma politiae ecclesiasticae, that governed the French Church of London thereafter. In 1561 he was one of the Reformed spokesmen at the Colloquy of Poissy before the French court. He ended his life as pastor and counsellor to Jeanne d'Albret in Béarn. He is the pattern of the lent minister, sent where the need was and handed back. “they sent forth Barnabas, that he should go as far as Antioch” (Act 11:22).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a colloquy as a conference or mutual discourse, and discipline as the government and correction exercised in a church.
webster_full: COL'LOQUY, n. Conversation; mutual discourse of two or more; a conference.
DIS'CIPLINE, n. In a church, the exercise of government and correction over its members.
DEL'EGATE, n. A person appointed and sent by another with powers to transact business as his representative.
FEL'LOWHELPER, n. A coadjutor; one who assists another in the same work.
scriptures: Then tidings of these things came unto the ears of the church which was in Jerusalem: and they sent forth Barnabas, that he should go as far as Antioch.

Then pleased it the apostles and elders, with the whole church, to send chosen men of their own company to Antioch with Paul and Barnabas; namely, Judas surnamed Barsabas, and Silas, chief men among the brethren:
Php 2:25
Yet I supposed it necessary to send to you Epaphroditus, my brother, and companion in labour, and fellowsoldier, but your messenger, and he that ministered to my wants.
We therefore ought to receive such, that we might be fellowhelpers to the truth.
corruption_summary: Geneva's minister lent to London to settle the French congregation.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The live misuse is in church practice rather than in the books: the modern assumption that a minister belongs to the congregation that pays him and that lending one out is a loss. Geneva sent its best men away repeatedly — to Paris, to London, to Béarn, to the Italian and Spanish congregations — and reckoned the whole Reformed communion its charge.

The principle to recover is that the churches are one body and may spend their men on one another's needs. Jerusalem did it without hesitation when it heard of Antioch: “they sent forth Barnabas, that he should go as far as Antioch” (Act 11:22). Paul did the same with Epaphroditus, and named him in both directions at once: “my brother, and companion in labour, and fellowsoldier, but your messenger” (Php 2:25).

pos: n. (Michelangelo Florio, c. 1515–after 1566, first minister of the Italian Church of London)
etymology: Italian Michelangelo, Michael the angel; Florio, from Latin flos, a flower.
biblical_def: Michelangelo Florio was a Tuscan of Jewish descent who became a Franciscan, came to the evangelical faith, was taken by the Roman Inquisition and held for twenty-seven months, escaped, and made his way through Naples, Lyons and Antwerp to England in 1550. Edward VI's council gave him the Italian stranger congregation in London and a pension, and Sir William Cecil took him into his house as an Italian tutor. In 1552 he was deposed from the ministry for fornication, which he confessed; he wrote to Cecil in terms of plain self-condemnation, was forgiven as a man and not restored as a minister, and continued as a tutor, writing an Italian grammar and a life of Lady Jane Grey, whom he had taught. Mary's accession drove him to the Grisons, where he pastored the Italian congregation at Soglio. His son John Florio became the lexicographer and the translator of Montaigne. The dictionary prints the fall because the sources do and because the handling of it was right. “He that covereth his sins shall not prosper: but whoso confesseth and forsaketh them shall have mercy” (Pro 28:13).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines to depose as to divest of office, and restoration as the act of replacing in a former state.
webster_full: DEPO'SE, v. To divest of office; to deprive of sovereignty or of ministry; to degrade.
RESTORA'TION, n. The act of replacing in a former state; renewal; recovery.
TU'TOR, n. A private instructor; one who has the care of a youth's education.
CONFES'SION, n. The acknowledgment of a crime, fault or sin; avowal.
scriptures: He that covereth his sins shall not prosper: but whoso confesseth and forsaketh them shall have mercy.
Create in me a clean heart, O God; and renew a right spirit within me.
Gal 6:1
Brethren, if a man be overtaken in a fault, ye which are spiritual, restore such an one in the spirit of meekness; considering thyself, lest thou also be tempted.
So that contrariwise ye ought rather to forgive him, and comfort him, lest perhaps such a one should be swallowed up with overmuch sorrow.
corruption_summary: The first Italian minister in London, deposed for sin he confessed and never restored.
corruption_paragraphs: Two bad instincts meet over a case like Florio's. One suppresses it, so that a congregation's founder appears in the record without the thing that ended his ministry; the other treats the deposition as proof that the whole Reformation was a hypocrisy. Neither is honest. He sinned, confessed without excuse, lost the office permanently, kept the fellowship of the church, and was employed in a work he could still be trusted with. That is what discipline looks like when it is working.

The principle to recover is that forgiveness and office are two different questions. The penitent is to be received and comforted — “ye ought rather to forgive him, and comfort him, lest perhaps such a one should be swallowed up with overmuch sorrow” (2Co 2:7) — and the restoration is to be done in a particular spirit: “restore such an one in the spirit of meekness; considering thyself, lest thou also be tempted” (Gal 6:1). None of that requires giving a man back the pulpit.
